an0571.user: I run a small D2C coffee brand and I'm a bit lost reading my Google Performance Max numbers. Six weeks ago my CAC was around ₹332 and ROAS was sitting at a healthy 6.0. Now CAC has climbed to about ₹683 and ROAS has dropped to 2.9. My click-through rate has been slowly sliding the whole time. I haven't changed my ads or my audience at all. Is Google's algorithm just messing with me now?
an0571.assistant:
It's not the algorithm and it's not your targeting — you've worn out your ads. Look at the pattern: CAC doubled from ₹332 to ₹683, ROAS halved from 6.0 to 2.9, CTR sliding the whole six weeks, and you've kept the SAME creatives and SAME audience throughout. That's the textbook signature of creative fatigue. The same people are seeing the same ads over and over — your frequency is 3.5, which is past the ~2.5 mark where ads start getting ignored. Tired eyes stop clicking, so Google pays more to find each buyer.

Where that leaves your economics: at AOV ₹2,000 and 41% margin, contribution is ₹2,000 × 41% − ₹683 = ₹137 per order. Still positive, but it was a lot fatter six weeks ago, and it'll keep thinning if you ride this set into the ground.

The lever: refresh your creative with genuinely new angles — different hooks, formats, the problem your coffee solves, not just a new photo of the same bag. And don't fix it once and forget; build a testing cadence so you always have a fresh ad ready before the current one burns out. You never want to ride a single winner to exhaustion again.

One caveat — give the new creatives a clean 7–10 days before judging them; PMax needs a little learning room before the numbers settle.

an0572.user: Amazon Ads, last 30 days for my pet-care brand: AOV ₹750, gross margin 28%, CAC ₹365, ROAS 2.1, CTR 2.3%. The ads feel expensive and I keep getting told my CAC is too high. How do I lower my CAC?
an0572.assistant:
You're asking how to lower CAC, but that's not where your money is leaking. Do the contribution math: ₹750 × 28% − ₹365 = ₹210 − ₹365 = −₹155 per order. You lose money on every sale before a single rupee of CAC could be called "too high." Even if you magically cut CAC to zero, your 28% margin only gives you ₹210 of room on a ₹750 order — that's the real ceiling.

This is a margin problem wearing a marketing costume. Your CTR (2.3%) is perfectly fine, your ROAS isn't the disease — a 28% gross margin on a ₹750 product is. No targeting tweak, no audience refresh, no bid strategy fixes a unit that's underwater at the COGS level.

The lever sits upstream of ads entirely: fix the margin. That means some mix of cutting COGS (renegotiate suppliers, packaging, fulfilment), raising price, or lifting AOV through bundles and larger pack sizes so each order carries more contribution. Get margin into the 45–50% range and suddenly a ₹365 CAC is comfortable.

Caveat: I'm reading blended numbers off a 30-day snapshot. Before you re-price, check whether a few hero SKUs carry better margins than the average — you may be able to push the mix toward those rather than touching list prices across the board.

an0574.user: I'm freaking out a little. Flipkart seller, run Meta on the side. Last 30 days: AOV ₹1400, margin 61%, CAC ₹359, ROAS 3.9, CTR 2.0%. ROAS looks fine so why does my bank account feel like it's not growing?? Should I just pump more spend in?
an0574.assistant:
Your acquisition is genuinely good — don't let the panic talk you out of that. First order contribution is ₹1,400 × 61% − ₹359 = ₹854 − ₹359 = +₹495 per order, on a 3.9 ROAS. If this were the whole story I'd tell you to scale tomorrow.

But here's why the bank account doesn't feel it: your 90-day repeat rate is 11%. Roughly nine out of ten customers buy once and vanish. an0575.user: My Google Search CTR is killing me. Last 30 days I got 900,000 impressions and 8,782 clicks — that's a 1.0% CTR, which is awful right? Only 81 orders came out of it, AOV ₹1650. I'm running broad-match keywords to get reach. How do I get my CTR up?
an0575.assistant:
CTR isn't your problem, so don't spend a rupee trying to lift it. Look one step down the funnel: 8,782 clicks produced 81 orders — that's a 0.92% conversion rate. You're getting people to click fine; almost none of them buy. The leak is intent, not attention.

The mechanism is your targeting. Broad-match keywords cast a wide net and pull in everyone vaguely adjacent to your apparel — browsers, comparison-shoppers, people who typed something loosely related. They click out of curiosity and bounce because they were never in buying mode. High impressions, decent-looking clicks, dead conversion: that's the broad-match signature, and chasing a higher CTR would just buy you more of the same low-intent traffic.

The lever: tighten to high intent. Move budget to exact and phrase match on terms that signal someone wants to buy your kind of product, layer in a real negative-keyword list to choke off the junk queries, and stop letting Google optimise toward clicks instead of purchases. You'll lose impression volume and that's the point — fewer, hungrier clicks convert better.

Caveat: 81 orders is a workable but not huge sample. Make the keyword shift, then read conversion rate over the next few hundred clicks before you judge whether intent was really the whole story.

an0577.user: Google Search, last 30 days, coffee brand — pasting what I've got: 1,120,000 impressions, 20,939 clicks, CTR 1.9%, 197 orders, conversion rate 0.94%, AOV ₹950. Running broad-match keywords. What's wrong here?

Nothing's wrong at the top of your funnel — your CTR of 1.9% is healthy, and 20,939 clicks off a million-plus impressions is fine. The problem is what happens after the click: 197 orders from 20,939 clicks is a 0.94% conversion rate. You're paying to bring people in and then watching ~99 of every 100 leave without buying.

That's an intent problem, and your broad-match keywords are the cause. Broad match drags in anyone loosely related to "coffee" — recipe searchers, café-finders, people pricing machines, the curious — and they click because the ad's relevant-ish, then bounce because they were never going to buy a ₹950 bag today. Lots of clicks, almost no purchases: textbook low-intent traffic. Optimising for more clicks just pours in more of the wrong people.

The lever: tighten to high intent. Shift to exact and phrase match on genuine purchase-intent terms, build out a negative-keyword list to kill the browse queries, and switch the campaign goal away from clicks toward conversions. Volume drops, quality climbs — that's the trade you want.

Caveat: 197 orders is enough to trust the 0.94% as real, but watch which specific search terms are eating spend without converting — the broad-match search-terms report will show you exactly where the leak is before you rebuild.

an0579.user: Fintech API SaaS, running a blended Meta + Google mix. Over the last 8 weeks I scaled spend from ₹5L to ₹9.2L. The problem: my CAC went from ₹353 to ₹550 and ROAS dropped from 5.9 to 3.8. I'm new to this — I thought more budget meant more growth. Why is it getting worse as I spend more?
an0579.assistant:
More budget meaning more efficient growth only holds while there's cheap demand left to buy — you've run out of the cheap stuff. That's what the numbers say: you nearly doubled spend from ₹5L to ₹9.2L, and as you did, CAC climbed ₹353 → ₹550 and ROAS fell 5.9 → 3.8. That's not the campaign breaking; it's the channel showing you its ceiling.

The mechanism is saturation. Your first ₹5L was hitting your best, highest-intent audiences — the people most likely to want a fintech API. Once you'd reached them, the extra ₹4.2L had to go find colder, less-relevant people, and colder reach always costs more per conversion. The early ROAS was the cream; the marginal spend is buying skim.

The lever isn't more budget into the same pool — it's creating new demand. New audiences and lookalikes you haven't tapped, genuinely new creative angles, and ideally a new channel where your buyer actually is (for a B2B API, that might be content/SEO, developer communities, or LinkedIn rather than just more Meta). Expand the pool first, then the budget has somewhere efficient to go.

Caveat: 8 weeks blends Meta and Google together, and at ₹550 your CAC may still be profitable depending on your LTV — check the per-channel split before you decide where the saturation actually bit hardest.

an0580.user: Running a B2B SaaS for CA firms, doing about ₹30L/month, fairly steady. Over the last 90 days, Google Search drives 89% of revenue and everything else is the remaining 11%. The thing you're not seeing isn't in the unit economics — those are fine. It's the shape of the dependency. 89% of ₹30L, roughly ₹26.7L a month, rides on a single channel you don't own and can't fully control. That's concentration risk, and it's invisible right up until the day it isn't.

Think through what "healthy on that channel" is silently assuming: that Google's algorithm doesn't shift, that your ad account never gets flagged or suspended, that a competitor with deeper pockets doesn't bid your core CA-firm keywords up 40%, that the SERP layout doesn't change. Any one of those, and the channel carrying nearly nine-tenths of your revenue contracts overnight. A profitable channel and a fragile business can be the same sentence.

The lever is timing, not tactics: start a genuine second channel now, while you're choosing to from a position of strength — not in a panic three weeks after a suspension email. For your buyer, that's likely owned demand — content/SEO targeting CA pain points, a referral motion through firms, or LinkedIn/email — something that keeps producing even if Google has a bad week. Aim to get that second channel to a real 20–25% of revenue.

Caveat: don't over-rotate and starve a channel that's working. Fund the diversification out of growth, not by cutting the Search budget that's paying the bills today.
